items.prompt: What does span of control measure?
choices: The count of projects that a team ships over each quarter
The count of people reporting directly to one manager
The count of management levels between an engineer and the CEO
items.explanation: Span is about direct reports to one manager.

items.prompt: Priya has a 180-minute weekly 1:1 budget and 10 reports. About how long does each get?
choices: 9 minutes
18 minutes
36 minutes
items.explanation: 180 divided by 10 is 18.

items.prompt: With a fixed 1:1 budget, what happens to time per report as the team grows?
choices: It grows
It shrinks
It stays exactly the same
items.explanation: A fixed pool divided among more people gives each a smaller share.

items.prompt: How many hours is a 180-minute weekly 1:1 budget?
choices: 2 hours
3 hours
4 hours
items.explanation: 180 divided by 60 is 3.

items.prompt: Besides short 1:1s, which symptom shows a span ceiling has been passed?
choices: The codebase compiles more slowly
Decisions pile up waiting on the manager
There are fewer meetings on everyone's calendar
items.explanation: Decision latency is the quieter symptom of a stretched manager.

items.prompt: Which range is a commonly quoted ceiling for hands-on technical management?
choices: Around 20 to 25 reports
Around 6 to 8 reports
Exactly 3 reports
items.explanation: It is a rule of thumb, not a law.

items.prompt: Does hiring more people into an over-stretched span fix the structure?
choices: Yes, because more hands will always clear the existing queue
No, it adds more people to the same queue
Yes, although only after the new people have been there a year
items.explanation: The queue is about decision routing, not hands.

items.prompt: Priya at 5 reports with a 180-minute budget: how long is each 1:1?
choices: 30 minutes
36 minutes
45 minutes
items.explanation: 180 divided by 5 is 36.

items.prompt: Priya raises her 1:1 budget from 180 to 240 minutes a week while at 12 reports. What does that change?
choices: Each report gets 15 minutes, and the structural bottleneck is gone
Each report gets 20 minutes, yet decisions still route through her
Each report gets 20 minutes, and the span ceiling no longer applies
Each report gets 24 minutes, but only if she stops doing code review
items.explanation: 240 divided by 12 is 20. More hours helps the 1:1s but does not change who decides what.
items.reference:
A fixed pool, divided
⏱ budget: 180 min of 1:1s per week
👥 5 reports: 36 min each
👥 11 reports: about 16 min each
👥 20 reports: 9 min each
Why: the budget does not grow with the team, so each added report thins everyone else's share.
items.learnMore:
Span of control is division

A manager's weekly 1:1 time is a fixed pool. Past the ceiling, the shortfall also shows up as decisions waiting on the manager.

Common mistake

Reading the ceiling as a verdict on effort. Working longer hours raises the pool a little but never fixes the structure.
items.reflection: Think of someone you know who answers to a very large group. Where did the thin attention show up first for the people reporting to them?

items.prompt: A lead has 10 reports who each own an area outright and need little day-to-day coaching. Which reading is most sound?
choices: The span is automatically a failure, since the ceiling is a hard limit of 8 reports
The span is fine only if the lead stops holding any 1:1s with the reports
The span is irrelevant, since coaching needs do not depend on the manager's time
A wider span can be sustainable here because the coaching load per person is low
items.explanation: The 6-to-8 figure is a rule of thumb for hands-on management. Low coaching demand can support a wider span.

items.prompt: Which pair of facts is a signal that a team should split?
choices: The team bought a new coffee machine and also added a second weekly standup
Everyone on the team has been working at the company for over a full year
Two workstreams share one reviewer and decisions all route through one person
items.explanation: Divergent workstreams on a shared decision-maker are structural signals.

items.prompt: How many possible pairs exist among 5 people?
items.explanation: 5 times 4 divided by 2 is 10.

items.prompt: How many possible pairs exist among 10 people?
items.explanation: 10 times 9 divided by 2 is 45.

items.prompt: Which formula gives the possible pairs among n people?
choices: n times n
2 times n
n times (n minus 1), divided by 2
items.explanation: Each person pairs with n-1 others, and each pair is counted twice.

items.prompt: Is headcount the only signal that a team may need to split?
choices: Yes, because only the count of people on the team ever matters
Yes, although only once the team goes beyond twenty people in total
No, workstreams, decisions and ownership matter as well
items.explanation: Headcount is the easiest signal, not the only one.

items.prompt: A team has one coherent workstream, a lead who decides routine things, and clear ownership. Is hiring likely enough?
choices: No, because every such team must split right now
No, because every such team must freeze all hiring
It may be, since the structural signals are missing
items.explanation: Without structural signals, the problem may only be capacity.

items.prompt: What does diffuse ownership look like?
choices: Every incident has one named owner at once
Incidents never happen on the team
After an incident nobody is sure whose fix it is
items.explanation: Unclear ownership shows up when something breaks.

items.prompt: What is onboarding drag?
choices: New hires finish their onboarding sooner than anyone had expected it
Onboarding takes exactly one single day for every new person who joins
New hires ramp slowly as too much context sits with one manager
items.explanation: Too much surface area for one person to hand off.

items.prompt: A team of 9 has one coherent workstream, a lead who handles routine calls, clear ownership, and 20-minute 1:1s. What is the soundest decision?
choices: Split now, because 9 is over the ceiling and the headcount number is the whole test
Split now, because every team above 8 people has diffuse ownership by default
Probably not yet: structural signals are absent, so hiring or waiting is defensible
Freeze hiring permanently, because the 1:1 time is below the 30-minute mark
items.explanation: The headcount number is a proxy. Without divergent work, bottlenecks or unclear ownership, there is no strong case.
items.reference:
Structural signals, not just a number
📏 span past the ceiling
🧩 divergent workstreams on one reviewer
🚦 decisions all route through one person
❓ nobody sure who owns an incident
Why: several of these together mean the structure is the problem; hiring only adds people to the same queue.
items.learnMore:
Pairs grow faster than people

The number of possible pairs among n people is n(n-1)/2, so 5 people have 10, 10 have 45, and 20 have 190. It is a proxy for coordination cost, not an exact count.

Common mistake

Treating a headcount number as the whole test. A small team with three structural signals can need a split before a large coherent one does.
items.reflection: Recall a group you were part of that felt too big or too tangled. Which of these signals could you actually see from the inside?

items.prompt: A team of 7 has two workstreams with different stakeholders, every decision routes through the manager, and nobody owns incidents. What follows?
choices: Consider a split despite the small headcount, since three structural signals show
Do not split, since 7 is below the commonly quoted ceiling of 8 direct reports
Hire two more engineers, since capacity is the one ingredient that is missing
Rotate the manager every month, since the person in the role is the real problem
items.explanation: Structural signals can justify a split below the typical number.

30 inside the two teams against 66 in one, though not everyone talks to everyone
30 inside the two teams against 66 in one, and the count is an exact measure

items.prompt: A functional team is grouped by what?
choices: Discipline, such as all backend engineers
Product area, with every skill included in it
Whichever office or time zone the people sit in
items.explanation: Functional means grouped by craft.

items.prompt: A cross-functional pod is grouped by what?
choices: An outcome or product area, with needed skills
A single discipline only, such as backend
The alphabetical order of all the surnames
items.explanation: A pod holds the mix of skills to ship an outcome.

items.prompt: What does a platform team provide?
choices: A capability that other teams consume
A feature only end customers see
A list of rules the other teams must obey
items.explanation: Platform teams serve other teams.

items.prompt: What is a strength of a functional team?
choices: Deep skill mentoring within a craft
Fastest end-to-end shipping of one feature
No need for any handoffs
items.explanation: People of one craft learn from each other.

items.prompt: What is a weakness of a pod?
choices: A thinner bench per discipline
Features need handoffs across several teams
No ownership of the outcome
items.explanation: Fewer peers of the same craft per pod.

items.prompt: Who are a platform team's customers?
choices: Other engineers and teams
Only the company's end users
Only the finance department
items.explanation: A platform's customers are internal.

items.prompt: All backend engineers in one team is which shape?
choices: Functional
Cross-functional pod
Platform
items.explanation: Grouped by discipline.

items.prompt: A team with frontend, backend and on-call all for payments is which shape?
choices: Cross-functional pod
Functional
Platform
items.explanation: It owns an outcome end to end.

items.prompt: Shipping one feature needs a frontend team and a backend team to hand work back and forth, and delivery is slow. Which change targets that cost?
choices: A bigger functional team with one more backend lead added on top of the existing ones
A platform team that reviews every handoff before it starts, one by one
A weekly status meeting between the frontend team and the backend team
A pod that holds both skills and owns one product area end to end
items.explanation: Pods remove handoffs by putting the skills in one team.
items.reference:
Three ways to draw the line
🛠 functional: grouped by discipline
🎯 pod: grouped by outcome, all skills inside
⚙ platform: provides a capability to other teams
Why: the shape decides which handoffs disappear and which skills get thinner.
items.learnMore:
Shape follows the work

Functional teams deepen craft; pods shorten the path from idea to shipped; platform teams multiply other teams. None is universally right.

Common mistake

Choosing a shape because it is fashionable. Look at whether the work divides more naturally by skill or by outcome.
items.reflection: Think of any group you know that is organised by skill and another organised by outcome. What does each do easily and what does it struggle with?

items.prompt: A small team has one product area but needs deep mentoring in a single specialty. Which shape fits best?
choices: Several pods, since every team of more than 3 people must be cross-functional
Functional, since craft depth matters and there is little to separate by outcome
A platform team, since a specialty is a capability consumed by other teams
No structure at all, since mentoring only ever happens between two people
items.explanation: Functional suits small teams or discipline-heavy work.

One pod for each script, so that each can diverge from the others freely

A sign the pods need more people before any other change is attempted

items.prompt: What does Conway's Law say?
choices: Bigger teams will always build much better systems than small ones
Systems tend to mirror how their organization communicates
Software is always designed in full before the org chart exists
items.explanation: Structure of the org shapes structure of the system.

items.prompt: Two pods with separate ownership and on-call tend to produce what over time?
choices: One single merged service
More separately deployable pieces of software
No services at all
items.explanation: Crossing the pod line is slightly harder, so interfaces form there.

items.prompt: If the org chart splits but the code stays one shared module, what remains?
choices: Nothing, the split fixes it fully
The coordination cost
Only the cost of one team
items.explanation: Teams still negotiate every change to the module.

items.prompt: Does Conway's Law require anyone to plan it?
choices: Yes, only when an architect plans it
No, it happens whether or not anyone plans it
Yes, only with a formal meeting
items.explanation: It emerges from communication friction.

items.prompt: Where do interfaces tend to settle after a split?
choices: Where the office floor ends
Where the team boundary falls
Wherever the oldest file is
items.explanation: Friction concentrates at the team boundary.

items.prompt: Two pods both edit one module daily. What does that suggest?
choices: The pods are already fully independent of each other
Coordination will continue across the pods
The module has no ownership issues left to resolve
items.explanation: Shared daily edits force shared decisions.

items.prompt: In which direction does Conway's Law cut?
choices: Only from the system to the org, and never in the other direction
Both ways: org shapes system, system shapes who talks
Neither way, because it is really only a joke about software
items.explanation: The influence runs both directions.

items.prompt: What should move together when a team splits?
choices: Only the org chart
The org split and the system boundary
Only the codebase
items.explanation: Moving one alone leaves coordination cost in place.

items.prompt: Two pods were created, but both still edit one monolithic module and two months later they block each other on merges. Best explanation?
choices: The org boundary moved but the system boundary did not, so coordination returned via shared code
The pods are too small, so the answer is to add several engineers to each of them
The pods were split on the wrong domain, so the answer is to simply rename them both
Merge conflicts happen only when two teams use different version control tooling
items.explanation: Conway's Law cuts both ways; the shared module keeps forcing the teams to coordinate.
items.reference:
Org chart and system, move together
👥 two pods, separate ownership
🔌 friction crossing the pod line
🧱 interfaces settle at the pod boundary
Why: systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the teams that build them.
items.learnMore:
Conway's Law cuts both ways

The org shapes the interfaces, and the interfaces then shape who must talk to whom. Splitting only one of the two leaves coordination cost in place.

Common mistake

Splitting the org chart and leaving one tightly coupled module that both teams edit daily. The coordination is only relabeled.
items.reflection: Think of a product you use that feels like several teams stitched together. Where did the seams fall, and who might have had to talk to whom?

items.prompt: A company wants five independent services but one team of five works on all of them as a single group. What does Conway's Law suggest?
choices: They will become cleanly independent services because the single team is so small
They will be independent only if the architecture diagram says that they should be
They will tend to stay tightly coupled unless ownership is separated too
They will split on their own as the team's workload grows over the next few months
items.explanation: Without separate ownership there is no communication friction to place the interfaces.

choices: Give each side its own owning team and on-call, then let the interface form between them
Write a rule document that forbids billing code from ever calling the search code
Put both on one team so that they can agree on the interface in an informal way
Keep a single team but ask its members to imagine that there are two separate teams
items.explanation: A boundary that is also an ownership boundary holds up under pressure.

A rule that only applies to software teams of more than a hundred people
A tendency driven by communication friction between teams, not a guarantee
A claim that architecture has to be designed before the org chart is drawn up

items.prompt: What is the best basis for a split line?
choices: Making both halves the same headcount
Alphabetical order of names
Domain or ownership boundaries
items.explanation: Coordination cost tracks who must talk to whom about decisions.

items.prompt: What goes wrong with an arbitrary 5 and 6 headcount split?
choices: Both pods immediately become fully independent of each other
Neither pod would need any lead to make decisions at all
Both pods still hold mixed payments and search work
items.explanation: Decisions still cross the pod line as often as before.

items.prompt: What must a new pod's lead have?
choices: Only a bigger title
No responsibility for the pod
Real decision authority over a bounded area
items.explanation: A lead without authority recreates the bottleneck.

items.prompt: What is the first transition step in the case?
choices: Closing the old repositories
A company-wide party
A written ownership doc per pod
items.explanation: It names services, on-call and stakeholders.

items.prompt: How long before the old rotation ends do the new on-call rotations start?
choices: One day
Six months
Two weeks
items.explanation: The overlap gives an incident two people who know what is happening.

items.prompt: When should the code-ownership file be updated?
choices: Weeks later, once things settle
Never, it is not needed
The same day as the announcement
items.explanation: Routing should match the new boundary immediately.

items.prompt: How did the month 9 split divide 11 engineers?
choices: Payments 8 and search 3
Payments 10 and search 1
Payments 6 and search 5
items.explanation: 6 plus 5 makes 11.

items.prompt: Why were both leads already the informal contact for their area?
choices: So nobody has to learn anything new
Because outside candidates are never allowed
So the split formalizes an existing pattern
items.explanation: Authority already exists in practice.

items.prompt: Priya names an assistant manager who handles some 1:1s but reports combined status to her. What does this fix?
choices: The decision bottleneck, since someone else now sits in the middle
Some 1:1 time, but decisions still route through Priya
Nothing at all, since 1:1 time is also unchanged
The ownership split, since there are now two managers
items.explanation: Ownership was never separated, so the bottleneck is merely one layer removed.
items.reference:
A split that works
🧭 split line: by domain, not even headcount
👤 leads: real authority, already trusted
📝 ownership doc, signed off by both leads
🔁 on-call overlap, ownership file same day
Why: a split reduces coordination only when the line, the authority and the routing all change together.
items.learnMore:
Announcing is not splitting

The org chart changes in a minute; the routing of reviews, pages and decisions takes deliberate steps to follow it.

Common mistake

Treating the announcement as the finish line. If tooling still routes to the old owner, decisions still bottleneck there.
items.reflection: Think of a change at work that was announced loudly. What had to change quietly in tools or habits before it was real?

items.prompt: Priya delays the code-ownership update for three weeks after announcing the split. What is the concrete risk?
choices: Engineers will be unable to commit code to either pod's repository for three weeks
The two leads will lose their formal authority over their pods until it is updated
Nothing, since routing follows the org chart automatically without any extra steps
Reviews and pages keep routing to the old owner, recreating the bottleneck
items.explanation: Tooling decides who gets paged, not the chart.

items.learnMore:
Announcing is not splitting

The org chart changes in a minute; the routing of reviews, pages and decisions takes deliberate steps to follow it.

Common mistake

Treating the announcement as the finish line. If tooling still routes to the old owner, decisions still bottleneck there.
items.reflection: Think of a change at work that was announced loudly. What had to change quietly in tools or habits before it was real?

items.prompt: The new pod needs confident calls from day one. Which lead choice does the case favor?
choices: An outside hire, since fresh eyes always make confident calls sooner than insiders do
An internal candidate already seen as the point of contact for the area
Whoever has the longest tenure, whatever their depth in the specific domain may be
Two co-leads sharing every single call, to avoid having any one person decide
items.explanation: Depth in the domain plus informal authority fits a fast start.
items.reference:
A split that works
🧭 split line: by domain, not even headcount
👤 leads: real authority, already trusted
📝 ownership doc, signed off by both leads
🔁 on-call overlap, ownership file same day
Why: a split reduces coordination only when the line, the authority and the routing all change together.

items.prompt: The combined on-call rotation ends the day the split is announced, with no overlap. What risk does that add?
choices: Engineers will be paged twice for every single incident during the first month
The old rotation will keep paging engineers who have already moved to new pods
Incidents become impossible to detect at all during the first week of the split
An incident in the gap meets one person still learning the rotation
items.explanation: The two-week overlap exists so two people know what is happening.

items.prompt: At month 18, how many engineers does the payments pod have?
items.explanation: Payments grew from 6 to 11.

items.prompt: About how long is each 1:1 at an 11-report lead with a 180-minute budget?
choices: 16 minutes
36 minutes
9 minutes
items.explanation: 180 divided by 11 is about 16.

items.prompt: Which two options does the payments pod face at month 18?
choices: Split it again, or keep one pod and add a leadership layer
Shrink the pod down to a single engineer, or else close it entirely
Merge it with the search pod, or else stop hiring altogether for good
items.explanation: Both resolve the span number.

items.prompt: Is one split a permanent fix?
choices: No, a growing pod can hit the ceiling again
Yes, splits last forever
Yes, as long as the leads are happy
items.explanation: Org design is a recurring decision.

items.prompt: What decides whether to split payments again?
choices: Whether payments has a separable sub-domain
Whether the engineers happen to like each other
Whether the day of the week happens to be a Friday
items.explanation: A real boundary makes a split clean.

items.prompt: What goes wrong when you split before signals appear?
choices: A pod too thin to be self-sufficient
The pod becomes too fast to measure
Every engineer is promoted
items.explanation: Fragmenting a team that still benefits from shared context.

items.prompt: At month 6 with 8 engineers, was waiting defensible?
choices: Yes, as a watched 'not yet'
No, the team must split immediately
No, hiring must stop immediately
items.explanation: Span was borderline and ownership mostly clear.

items.prompt: After the month 9 split, whom does Priya manage?
choices: The two pod leads
All 11 engineers as before
Only new hires
items.explanation: She now manages leads, not individual engineers.

items.prompt: The payments pod of 11 contains two sub-domains, core payments and fraud, with different stakeholders and failure modes. What is the strongest move?
choices: Add a leadership layer but keep every decision inside one single large pod
Do nothing at all, since a pod can never exceed a headcount of exactly 11
Split again along that line, since a real separable boundary exists
Merge fraud into search to even out the headcount between the two pods
items.explanation: A separable sub-domain makes a clean second split possible.
items.reference:
The ceiling returns
🔁 month 9: 11 reports, about 16 min each
🔁 month 18: payments pod at 11 again
🔀 option A: split again along a sub-domain
🪜 option B: keep one pod, add a leadership layer
Why: growth brings back the same arithmetic, and the right fix depends on whether a separable boundary exists.
items.learnMore:
Org design is recurring

A pod that keeps growing hits the same ceiling; the second time there is a management layer to use and a new choice to make.

Common mistake

Treating one split as a permanent fix. Keep watching the signals as the pods grow.
items.reflection: Think of a group you know that reorganized once and then grew again. What signals told you it might be time to reorganize a second time?

items.prompt: The payments pod of 11 is one coherent domain with no natural sub-boundary, simply grown large. Which option fits best?
choices: Keep one pod and add a second layer of leadership under its lead
Split anyway along an arbitrary line of 5 engineers and 6 engineers
Reduce the pod to 6 by moving five of its engineers over to search
Wait for a third pod to appear without taking any action at all today
items.explanation: Without a boundary, an arbitrary split recreates coordination cost; a layer fixes the span.

items.prompt: Both pods modify a shared risk-scoring module weekly and neither owns it. What is the most sensible response?
choices: Merge the two pods back together so that they can share the module once more
Let both pods keep editing it and hope the conflicts will resolve themselves
Give the module a single owner and treat it as a platform-like capability
Freeze all changes to the module permanently, so that nobody can break it
items.explanation: A shared dependency recreates the coordination the split was meant to remove.

The split will cost nothing, since splitting is always reversible overnight

items.explanation: Splitting on anticipated growth fragments shared context.
